new_en: Menachos 29, in Shimusha Rabba; Rosh, and so it also appears from the words of Rambam.
Rambam, chapter 4 of Hilchot Tefillin; R' Manoach.

"Fit to write tefillin." All of this concerns a full convert. Regarding a ger toshav, Pri Megadim, Levush Serad, Machatzit HaShekel, and many others agree that he is invalid because he is not subject to the mitzvah of binding tefillin. Shaarei Teshuvah proposes a novel interpretation, that Darchei Moshe's validation refers to a ger toshav who accepted all the mitzvot except the prohibition of neveilah, so that he is subject to tefillin. In my humble opinion this too is incorrect, because in any event he is not commanded in binding tefillin. If voluntary acceptance were enough, then a woman or a slave who accepted the mitzvah of tefillin upon themselves would become fit to write tefillin, which is untenable. One cannot answer that women are protested against for wearing tefillin, as stated above in siman 38, because that is only an extra stringency based on concern for the Pesikta, whereas our Talmud holds that we do not protest, as Beit Yosef states there. Slaves likewise prove the point, since they are not protested against, as I wrote above in Mishnah Berurah in the name of Tosefet Shabbos. Likewise, according to this reasoning, if a woman undertook the mitzvah of tzitzit she would be fit even according to Rabbeinu Tam to make tzitzit for men. This cannot be correct, for then Rabbeinu Tam would agree in such a case and the Rosh's proof from Gittin 45b, from the basket of the wife of R' Chanina ben Dosa that she would one day place techelet in it for the righteous in the future, would fall away. Beyond all this, conversion cannot be partial; see Masekhet Gerim. Furthermore, one who underwent brit milah but did not immerse, regarding whom the Rosh writes in Avodah Zarah that he is no worse than a ger toshav because he accepted all the mitzvot, would according to this logic be fit to write sacred texts and, according to R' Yitzchak's view that slaughter depends on belonging to the class obligated in slaughter, would be fit to slaughter as a Jew. Yet the plain Gemara in Yevamos 46, which says, "since he did not immerse he is a non-Jew," implies otherwise.

"For the need of his fellow, they are as the feet of the one who drew the water." See Mishnah Berurah, where we wrote that some disagree. The Mechaber's position is based on Rabbeinu Tam, Rosh, and Ran. Ra'ah in his novellae to Beitzah also maintains Rabbeinu Tam's position, though he inclines to say that while the water is treated as the feet of the one who drew it, it must also be restricted by the techum of the person for whom it was drawn, so that the recipient may bring it only to a place permitted to both. His reasoning is understandable in light of Rashba's challenge to Rabbeinu Tam. In truth, however, most Rishonim disagree and hold that the water is as the feet of the person for whom it was drawn, because we rule throughout the Talmud that one who lifts a found object for his fellow effects acquisition for his fellow. This is the view of Rashi and Rashbam cited by Tosafos, and R' Chananel rules likewise. The wording cited in Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of R' Chananel is difficult and may contain a scribal error. Baal HaMaor and Ra'avad likewise hold this view, as does Rashba in his novellae, where he discusses the matter at length and challenges Rabbeinu Tam. Meiri inclines likewise. Maggid Mishneh writes that this is also the view of Rambam and Rif, who omitted this particular ruling because they relied upon the established principle that one who lifts a found object for his fellow effects acquisition for his fellow. This explanation of their omission is more satisfactory than Ran's suggestion that they ruled like R' Shimon and relied upon the anonymous Mishnah concerning the well of the Babylonian pilgrims being as the feet of the one who draws from it, without distinguishing whether he draws for himself or for another. Riaz also follows this position, though he states it specifically after the water was given to the recipient and explains it through acquisition from hefker, following the wording of the sugya in Beitzah. Under the general rule that one who lifts a found object for his fellow effects acquisition, however, that further transfer is unnecessary. It is possible that Riaz agrees and merely copied the formulation of the sugya. The approach of Rivav on Rif likewise rules that the water is as the feet of the person for whom it was drawn. Eliyah Rabbah and Nahar Shalom discuss nearly all these points, though they frame the law after the water has already reached the recipient. From all these Rishonim, however, it appears that even while the water is still in the hand of the person who drew it, he may not carry it according to his own techum but only according to the techum of the person for whom he drew it, because it already belongs to that recipient. Avodat HaKodesh's wording that he "gave it to his fellow" merely follows the Gemara's formulation; the same law applies even before actual delivery. Accordingly, it is reasonable to rule not like the Mechaber but that the water follows the recipient's techum, particularly once it has already reached him, where Riaz is explicit and Bach also agrees. Indeed, there is even stronger reason to treat it as the recipient's feet once it is in his possession than while it remains with the drawer. See Rashba's novellae and his questions on Rabbeinu Tam.

(1) "Long and narrow." Its width is less than its length. (2) "And not aligned with the square of the earth." Its north side does not face true north and its south side true south; rather, it stands diagonally. (3) "4 equal corners." This excludes a city that is wider on 1 side and narrower on the other, which does not have equal corners and is not a true square. It is squared as explained in seif 4. (4) "As it is." If it is long and narrow, we do not enlarge its width to equal its length. Likewise, if it is not aligned with the cardinal directions, we do not enlarge it in order to realign its square with the cardinal directions, unlike the case in seif 3.

"4 amot by 4 amot." See Magen Avraham, who writes that if a structure does not have a width of 4 amot, no matter how long it is, it is not called a house. I did not copy this ruling because the later authorities challenged it and hold that the matter depends upon the dispute cited in Yoreh De'ah, siman 286, seif 13, and Shach there, regarding mezuzah. "And storehouses." The same law applies to horse stables that contain a residential dwelling. [Gemara] "A roof and plastered ceiling." Gra writes that the word "plastered ceiling" should not be in the text, because it is absent from both the Gemara and the codifiers. Regarding houses that project outward one after another, the measuring and squaring of the city depends upon the placement of those houses in relation to the city's main body. Where they project opposite the central portion of the city there is greater room to include them within the city's square. Rashba's novellae support such a distinction, and Rambam and Ra'avad may also agree. Where houses project only from 1 side, the positions attributed to Ra'ah and Ra'avad, as cited by Ritva, indicate that the city is squared by drawing the appropriate imaginary lines around those projections. This is also discussed by Gaon Yaakov and Yad Ephraim. The reading that would produce a diagonal extension of less than 4,000 amot is therefore not decisive. The city must instead be squared afterward in accordance with the method of the Rishonim cited by the later authorities, as explained in Mishnah Berurah.
